variable: beat_3_9s: a second concrete surprise / test / visual reveal between about 3 and 9 s (variant) vs the factory's normal post-hook structure (control)
hypothesis: Among viewers who stay past the opening, a second surprise in the 3-9 s window keeps more of them at 8 s than the normal setup/explanation beat (audit 2026-10-13: 30-53 points lost at 4-8 s).

schedule.note: planned; actual publish times are recorded by `experiment.py link`. Published or scheduled videos are not touched.

shared_rules: Every claim must pass the RESEARCH gate; if a planned line is not supported, reword it rather than keep it.
No new topic: the topic and angle are fixed by the experiment.

arm_rules.control: Claim-first opening; normal post-hook structure in 3-9 s; payoff and loop ending.
arm_rules.variant: Claim-first opening; a second concrete surprise, test or visual reveal in 3-9 s; no hook repeat, setup, definitions or jargon there; payoff and loop ending.

pairs.match_rationale: Both are eye/vision illusions with an at-home test, similar complexity (one mechanism), same 'your senses lie' series, human_body/visual category.

topics.topic: Why don't you notice the blind spot in each of your eyes?
topics.angle: Where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no light-sensing cells, so each eye has a gap in its view; the brain fills it in from the surroundings and from the other eye.
topics.opening_line: Each of your eyes has a hole.
topics.frame0_visual: a big doodle eye with a black hole in the middle of what it sees
topics.variant_beat_3_9: Test it now: close your left eye, stare at the cross with your right eye and move closer; the dot to its right vanishes (show the cross-and-dot test card filling the screen).

claims.claim: The optic disc has no photoreceptors, so part of each eye's visual field is blind.
The blind spot lies about 12-15 degrees toward the outer (temporal) side of the field of view.
The brain fills the gap using surrounding detail and the other eye.

revisions: Audit draft 'Two holes, your whole life' kept only as a loop idea; opening shortened to 6 words.

topics.topic: Why do you see a ghost color after staring at something red?
topics.angle: After staring at red, the visual system's response to red adapts and weakens, so on a white page the opposite colour of the red-cyan pair wins for a few seconds.
topics.opening_line: That cyan ghost isn't really there.
topics.frame0_visual: a red dot beside a faint cyan ghost dot on a white page
topics.variant_beat_3_9: Try it: stare at the red dot for 20 seconds, then look at the white side; a cyan dot appears that the screen never showed.

claims.claim: Negative afterimages appear in the complementary colour; red pairs with cyan in opponent-process accounts.
They arise from adaptation in the retina after prolonged exposure.

revisions: Idea file said 'green ghost' for red: corrected to cyan.
Idea file said 'the cones get tired': reworded to adaptation (the sources describe retinal adaptation and opponent channels, not simple cone fatigue).

pairs.match_rationale: Both are about what a mirror shows you, with a mirror test the viewer can do at once; similar complexity; human perception.

topics.topic: Why does a mirror swap left and right but not top and bottom?
topics.angle: A plane mirror reverses front and back (the direction perpendicular to it). The left-right swap is in our heads: we imagine turning around to stand where the reflection is.
topics.opening_line: Mirrors don't flip left and right.
topics.frame0_visual: a person facing a mirror, an arrow pointing into the glass and its reflection pointing back out
topics.variant_beat_3_9: Raise your right hand: the reflection's raised hand is on the same side as yours. Point at the mirror: the reflection points straight back at you. Front and back flipped, not left and right.

claims.claim: A plane mirror reverses the direction perpendicular to its surface (front-back), not left-right.
The perceived left-right swap comes from mentally turning around into the reflection's position.

revisions: Audit wording kept; 'writing looks reversed because you turned the page' kept as payoff.

topics.topic: Why can't you see your own eyes move in a mirror?
topics.angle: During fast eye movements (saccades) the brain briefly suppresses vision, so the motion of your own eyes is edited out; someone watching you sees them move.
topics.opening_line: You can't watch your own eyes move.
topics.frame0_visual: a face in a mirror, eyes mid-dart, a blank flash covering the movement
topics.variant_beat_3_9: Try it: in a mirror, look from your left eye to your right eye. You never see them move, but a friend beside you does.

claims.claim: Saccadic masking suppresses visual processing during rapid eye movements, so observers cannot see their own eyes move in a mirror.
An external observer clearly sees the eyes move.

revisions: Idea hook 'Your brain hides your eye movements from you' shortened to a 7-word assertion.

pairs.match_rationale: Both are everyday-sky space topics a viewer can check by looking up; one mechanism each; similar length of explanation.

topics.topic: Why do we only see one side of the Moon?
topics.angle: Earth's tides slowed the Moon's spin until one rotation takes as long as one orbit (tidal locking), so the same face points at us; slight rocking (libration) lets us see about 59% over time.
topics.opening_line: The Moon always shows us one face.
topics.frame0_visual: Earth and the Moon, one crater on the Moon marked and pointing at Earth
topics.variant_beat_3_9: But it does spin: exactly once per orbit, so the marked crater keeps facing us all the way round (animate the Moon circling with the crater always pointing at Earth).

claims.claim: The Moon is tidally locked: it rotates once per orbit, so one face points toward Earth.
Because of libration, about 59% of the Moon's surface can be seen from Earth over time.

revisions: Audit line 'You have never seen the back of the Moon' rejected (spacecraft and astronauts have; libration shows ~59%). 'Always shows us one face' kept: true for the near side.

topics.topic: Where do the stars go when the Sun is up?
topics.angle: They are still there: sunlight scattered by the atmosphere makes the daytime sky far brighter than starlight, so the stars are drowned out.
topics.opening_line: The stars never leave in the morning.
topics.frame0_visual: a bright blue daytime sky with faint stars drawn behind the glare
topics.variant_beat_3_9: Proof: telescopes with cameras still record bright stars in broad daylight; the stars never left, the sky just got brighter.

claims.claim: Stars are hidden in daytime because the atmosphere scatters sunlight into a bright glow that overwhelms faint starlight.
Astronomers measure bright stars during the day with telescopes and digital detectors.

revisions: Variant reveal limited to instrument detection (not naked-eye viewing), as the source describes.
